name: Gliding / sliding cupping

lead: Gliding or sliding cupping is a version of cupping therapy where the skin is oiled and a cup creating mild suction is moved across it instead of staying in one spot. It is used in traditional Chinese medicine and in massage-style cupping on the back, limbs and sometimes the face.

Practitioners use it to relax muscle and stimulate skin circulation, which people associate with a refreshed look and less tension. A 2026 randomised trial tested sliding cupping against narrowband UVB in plaque psoriasis, which is a skin-condition application.

paras: A therapist applies oil, creates suction in a cup (by pump, flame or heat in traditional versions) and glides it over an area for roughly 10 to 20 minutes. Facial and body versions use smaller cups with lighter suction.

Cupping can leave circular marks or bruises, and fire cupping has caused burns. It may worsen eczema or psoriasis in some people, and people with heart conditions or high blood pressure are advised by some health ministries to be cautious.

angle.text: Practitioners say the suction lifts and mobilises skin and muscle, giving a massage effect and a flushed, refreshed look. On the face, users aim for less puffiness and a brighter complexion; on the body the technique is used for tension relief.

lead: Gliding or sliding cupping is a form of cupping therapy in which oil or cream is applied to the skin and a suction cup is moved across it instead of being left in one place. Wikipedia describes the gliding variant as using massage oil so the cups can travel over muscle groups, in contrast with dry, fire and wet cupping.  The same movement, performed with small soft silicone cups, is the basis of facial cupping, a skincare routine popular on social media. [1]

People use it for two appearance-related reasons. On the body, practitioners use gliding cups as a massage-style way to ease muscle tightness and bring blood to the skin. [2] On the face, advocates say the lifting and gliding motion boosts circulation, relaxes facial muscles and reduces puffiness, giving a more radiant, de-puffed look. [1]

Research specific to sliding cupping is limited; a 2026 randomised trial in Medicine compared it with narrowband UVB phototherapy in 60 people with plaque psoriasis. [3] Broader reviews of cupping, summarised on Wikipedia, describe poor study quality and low-to-moderate evidence for musculoskeletal pain, and the American Cancer Society states that available evidence does not support health-benefit claims.  Dermatologists quoted in the press describe the facial version as low-risk when gentle and attribute its benefits mainly to temporary circulation and drainage effects. [1]

paras: In sliding cupping, the practitioner applies oil, creates suction inside a cup and moves it across the skin. Wikipedia lists dry, fire, wet and gliding cupping as the main types: fire cupping burns alcohol inside the cup to create negative pressure as it cools, wet cupping draws blood through small incisions, and the gliding type uses massage oil to move the cups over muscle groups.  Global News described modern practitioners as using either silicone cups tightened with a pump or heated glass cups. [2]

Practitioners of traditional Chinese medicine explain the technique as dispelling stagnation and improving the flow of qi, while other proponents describe it as stimulating circulation and relaxing tight muscle. [2] For facial use, a cream or oil such as argan, jojoba or grapeseed is applied so that soft silicone or glass cups can glide without pulling, with the suction lifting the tissue as the cup moves. [1]

Cupping's origins are unclear. Wikipedia notes that Hippocrates reportedly used it, that Islamic hadith contain early references to wet cupping (hijama), that the Taoist Ge Hong (281 to 341 AD) gives the earliest recorded Chinese use, and that Chinese hospitals have used it since the 1950s.  Finland has practised wet cupping since the 15th century, traditionally in saunas.

Body cupping reached a global audience at the 2016 Rio Olympics, when swimmer Michael Phelps appeared with circular marks on his back. [2] Wikipedia lists other athletes and celebrities associated with cupping, including Shaquille O'Neal, DeMarcus Ware, Natalie Coughlin and, more recently, Ben Shelton.  Global News reported that physiotherapist Michael Kay saw cupping as an extension of massage, saying 'Most physiotherapists use cupping as an extension for muscle relief.' [2]

Facial cupping followed as a beauty trend. A HuffPost UK explainer says it spread on social media as a skincare step and that acupuncturist Paige Yang traces it to the Qing Dynasty under Empress Dowager Cixi as a gentler alternative to body cupping. [1] Looksmaxxing communities mention cupping-style face and neck massage among skin and facial-puffiness routines, though dedicated threads are sparse.

Proponents of the facial version say it improves circulation and blood flow, relieves tension in the jaw and sinus areas, supports lymphatic drainage, reduces inflammation and puffiness, and leaves skin looking radiant. [1] Cosmetic dermatologist Michele Green is quoted suggesting evening use to reduce overnight swelling. [1]

For body use, practitioners say suction widens blood vessels, speeds recovery and gently stretches tight muscle. [2] Traditional explanations refer to removing stagnant blood or 'toxins', which skeptics such as James Hamblin and Steven Novella have disputed in print, noting that a cupping bruise is a blood clot rather than flowing blood.

General descriptions say practitioners continually move the cup rather than leaving it fixed, use light suction on thin facial skin, and treat each area for a few minutes; body massage cupping is described as lasting roughly 10 to 20 minutes. [1] Silicone cups are described as forgiving for beginners and easy to clean. [1] Interview sources advise learning from licensed practitioners rather than influencers. [1]

The 2026 trial in Medicine enrolled 60 patients with plaque psoriasis and tested whether sliding cupping was non-inferior to narrowband UVB phototherapy in improving disease severity. [3] It addresses a skin condition rather than cosmetic outcomes.

Reviews summarised on Wikipedia report that cupping evidence is of poor quality with inconsistent blinding, that benefit for musculoskeletal and myofascial pain is low to moderate and may not differ from placebo, and that evidence for acne is lacking.  Global News cited two 2012 studies, one in knee arthritis with less pain after four months though patients knew their treatment, and one in 61 people with chronic neck pain in which cupping and progressive muscle relaxation performed similarly. [2] No published randomised trial of facial cupping for wrinkles, puffiness or skin tone was found.

Suction breaks small capillaries, producing circular bruises or petechiae that typically fade within a few days. [2] Wikipedia lists scarring, burns, skin darkening, ulcers, possible infection and worsened eczema or psoriasis as reported effects, with higher risk for fire and wet cupping.  The Cambodian health ministry has warned that cupping can be dangerous for people with high blood pressure or heart problems.

For facial use, the HuffPost UK piece reports that practitioners advise waiting about three weeks after Botox and six weeks after filler, avoiding open sores, active acne, sunburn and recently treated skin, and using caution on blood thinners. Green warned that improper cupping can cause broken capillaries and may irritate rosacea or acne-prone skin, and that repetitive suction might break down collagen. [1]

A 2026 randomised trial published in Medicine enrolled 60 patients with plaque psoriasis and tested sliding cupping against narrowband UVB phototherapy for non-inferiority. [3] Broader cupping reviews report poor study quality and low-to-moderate evidence for pain.  No studies of sliding cupping for facial appearance were found.

lore.intro: Gliding cupping is discussed mainly as a skincare and massage practice, with practitioners and beauty writers making claims about circulation and puffiness. [1]
